item.title: Do Partners Need to Love Each Other Equally?
item.description:
Relationships

Do Partners Need to Love Each Other Equally?

Unequal love does not always imply an unhealthy relationship.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Mutual love is essential, but precisely equal amounts of love are neither necessary nor possible.
  • Greater relational power may increase temptation, but temptation need not result in infidelity.
  • A small asymmetry in love is tolerable, or even enriching; a large gap can undermine intimacy and commitment.

"Just because someone doesn't love you the way you think they should, doesn't mean they don't love you with everything they have."—Mary O.

"If equal affection cannot be, let the more loving one be me."—W. H. Auden

Equality is a central value in human life and romantic relationships. Partners often resemble one another in political and social values, religiosity, education, personal history, smoking habits, and IQ. Such similarities facilitate mutual understanding and shared activities.

But must partners also love each other equally? I suggest not. Mutual love is essential, but precisely equal amounts of love are neither necessary nor possible. The crucial question is not whether partners love equally, but whether any difference is small enough to sustain an enduring and flourishing relationship.

Measuring Love

"Love always differs, but everyone deserves a partner who puts in equal effort, most of the time. Love is less about the partner's achievements and more about their attitude and intentions toward you."—Anonymous

Source: Michael Morse / Pexels

Measuring how much one partner loves another is difficult. Unlike researchers, ordinary people cannot rely on physiological indicators. Instead, they depend on their own feelings and their partner's behavior, often perceiving differences that may be real, exaggerated, or simply a reflection of different love languages.

People discussing unequal love often describe both sides as painful. One partner may feel they love more and are therefore more vulnerable; the other may feel guilty for not reciprocating to the same degree. Yet many people note that partners can love differently without loving inadequately. This distinction is crucial: Unequal love does not necessarily imply an unhealthy relationship. One partner may love somewhat more deeply while the other still loves deeply enough for the relationship to thrive. The problem is not inequality itself, but inequality that becomes substantially disturbing.

Romantic Inequality and Infidelity

"In a romantic relationship, you're on the same team. You should never try to win, because if you win, your partner loses."—Anonymous

Inequality becomes problematic when it is accompanied by a sense of undeserved inferiority or superiority. The partner who feels less valued may experience jealousy, envy, or resentment, while the partner who feels superior may believe that more attractive alternatives are available.

Research has linked relationship inequality and power differences to instability and infidelity. Lower levels of infidelity have been found in more equal romantic partnerships (Prins et al., 1993), and greater perceived relationship power has been associated with increased interest in alternative partners, including romantic thoughts, desires, and actual interactions (Birnbaum et al., 2025).

These findings help explain why differences in love can matter. The less-invested partner often possesses greater relational power because they have less to lose if the relationship ends. Lower emotional investment may make someone more willing to risk the relationship, whereas the more loving partner may act more cautiously because the potential loss is greater. Still, greater power may increase temptation without resulting in infidelity. Commitment, moral values, empathy, and concern for the partner can prevent temptation from becoming behavior.

Is There an Optimal Gap in Love?

"The best marriages are not 50/50, but ones in which both partners think they are giving 60 percent."—Popular relational advice

"My wife wants sex in the back of the car, and she wants me to drive."—Rodney Dangerfield

Research suggests that moderate differences in desirability can sometimes be attractive. High-achieving men, for example, often report wanting to marry women who are as smart as, or smarter than, themselves, viewing this as beneficial to both the relationship and themselves (Whelan, 2006). Other research suggests that men and women tend to pursue partners who are, on average, about 25 percent more desirable than themselves (Bruch & Newman, 2018). A moderate difference in desirability can foster admiration and enhance self-esteem. Similarly, a moderate difference in the amount of love may be tolerable and perhaps even enriching. We cannot fully control how much we love another person, nor can we determine exactly how much another person will love us. Expecting perfect symmetry is therefore unrealistic (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019).

What we can reasonably expect is mutuality: Each partner should love the other enough for the relationship to matter profoundly to them. The difference between loving 55 percent and 45 percent is largely meaningless because love is not a measurable commodity. What matters more is whether both partners are motivated primarily by giving rather than by calculating what they receive. Once lovers start keeping score, intimacy can become a competition.

Here lies a paradox: Romantic equality does not require equal amounts of love. A relationship can tolerate, and perhaps even benefit from, a small asymmetry. At different times, the balance may even shift. What matters is that both partners experience the relationship as deeply meaningful.

A large gap is different. When one partner loves deeply while the other merely enjoys being loved, the relationship becomes fundamentally unequal. The more loving partner may become anxious and dependent, while the less-loving partner acquires disproportionate power. Under such circumstances, the imbalance can undermine both intimacy and commitment. Accordingly, our goal should not be equality in the amount of love, but equality in the significance of the relationship to both partners.

Concluding Thoughts

"It doesn't matter if I love him more than he loves me. It only matters that he loves me as much as he can."—Anonymous

Romantic partners naturally want to be loved, but they need not be loved in exactly equal measure. Exact equality is probably impossible, and attempts to measure it too precisely may themselves be harmful. What matters is not identical intensity but sufficient mutuality. Each partner should feel deeply valued, cared for, and committed to. Some asymmetry is inevitable, and a small amount may even enrich a relationship. The danger arises when the gap becomes so large that one partner is devoted while the other merely enjoys being loved. The healthiest romantic relationships, therefore, are not necessarily those in which partners love equally, but those in which both partners love enough. Romantic equality lies not in equal amounts of love, but in the equal significance of the relationship to both partners.

item.title: Joy Prepares Our Minds and Bodies for Learning
item.description:
Play

Joy Prepares Our Minds and Bodies for Learning

Positive emotions unlock the brain's potential through the arts and play.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Artistic experiences physically, socially organize children's attention, emotion, neurological engagement.
  • Infusing routines and learning with imagination, movement may transform resistance into joyful connection.
  • Broaden-and-Build Theory shows how positive emotions foster lasting cognitive and social resources.
Teaching and learning. What joy!
Source: Literacy@Play; used with permission.

When Katie Bernstein was a preschool teacher, the most difficult part of her day was the long walk down the hallway to the playground. Staying quiet past all the classrooms and the front office was simply too much for a group of excited 3-year-olds eager to get outside. The daily transition often became stressful for everyone involved.

Then one day, a veteran teacher transformed the situation entirely.

“Shhhh,” she whispered dramatically to the children. “Do you know about the tigers?”

The children froze.

“You’re in the jungle,” she continued. “There’s a mama tiger and her babies sleeping nearby. We have to tiptoe quietly so we don’t wake them.”

Suddenly, the hallway changed. Smiles spread across the children’s faces as they pantomimed “shhhhh” to one another. In exaggerated tiptoes, children moved silently, carefully, and joyfully down the hall. What had moments earlier required correction and control now emerged naturally through imagination and shared play. The children were no longer simply “behaving.” They were engaged. Focused. Regulated. Connected to a shared experience and common goal.

Pretending together transformed a stressful transition into a joyful moment. And joy expanded what the children were capable of doing.

As educators, artists, researchers, and parents, we have become increasingly interested in these moments of joy—not as extras or rewards attached to learning, but as conditions that help make learning possible in the first place.

Sing!
Source: Sara Sherman/Mozart for Munchkins; Used with permission

When Stress Shuts Down Learning (and Joy Reignites It)

When humans experience intense negative emotions or a stressful regulation challenge (like walking quietly down the hall for a preschooler), the prefrontal cortex—the part of our brains responsible for reasoning—goes offline. Instead, our amygdalas take charge, readying us for survival through fight or flight. This is one reason why tasks that are too challenging do not promote learning: When children are challenged to the point of frustration and confusion, they are not ready for creativity or innovation. Instead, they are likely to disengage, and disengagement means poorer learning outcomes.

article continues after advertisement

The opposite is true for positive emotions. Positive emotions, such as joy, create favorable conditions for exploration, flexible thinking, and learning. Instead of narrowing our attention toward an immediate threat, positive emotions broaden our sense of what is possible. Joy invites us to play, experiment, and try new ways of acting.

The Broaden-and-Build Power of Positive Emotions

These ideas are central to Barbara Fredrickson’s Broaden-and-Build Theory, which explains how positive emotions influence learning through a two-step process. First, positive emotions broaden our immediate thoughts and actions. For Katie’s students, the joy of pretending to walk through the jungle drew them into a shared imaginary world. Their desire not to wake the mama tiger and her babies motivated them to pay close attention, walk with control and purpose, and keep their voices quiet.

Second, these actions build lasting cognitive, social, physical, and emotional resources. By joyfully practicing how to manage their voices, bodies, and attention towards a shared goal, Katie’s students developed skills they could use beyond the game itself. Each day, as the class made its way outside, they recalled the imaginary jungle and recreated those same purposeful actions. The joyful experience did more than motivate the children in the moment; it gave them a shared experience they could draw on to regulate their behavior and work toward a collective goal in the future: learning how to walk quietly down the hall to play outside.

Rantala and Määttä wrote in their “Ten Theses of the Joy of Learning at Primary Schools” that “a school is not a desert of emotion.” We can’t separate how we think, how we perceive the world, and how we are motivated from our emotions.

Source: Sara Sherman/ Mozart for Munchkins/ Used with permission

Making the Connection Visible Through the Arts

The arts make this relationship especially visible. Art is designed to evoke emotion, giving educators a powerful way to create emotional experiences that capture attention, foster connection, and allow children to make and share meaning with others.

Anyone who has worked with children has seen this play out in real time. At Mozart for Munchkins concerts, children often respond to music before adults even realize they are participating. A toddler begins conducting before they fully understand what a conductor is. A shy child slowly inches closer to a cello, mesmerized by the vibration of the strings. Entire families begin swaying together unconsciously to the same pulse. In these moments, music organizes attention and emotion socially, physically, and neurologically all at once.

Joy is therefore not something added after learning. From Mozart for Munchkins to the hallway-turned-jungle in Katie’s preschool, joy is what draws children into the experience and makes learning possible. So how can we create joy… at home, in the classroom, and when we don’t realize we even need it?

article continues after advertisement
  • Notice moments of wonder.
  • Leave space for imagination. A hallway might become a jungle, the piano might turn into the sound of waves, and rhythm can become a story.
  • Add rhythm and movement to learning. Clapping, swaying, tapping, or conducting along to music can help organize focus and engagement.
  • Sing together, even if it’s imperfect and messy.
  • Return to familiar songs and stories. Repetition often deepens comfort, confidence, and connection.
  • Remember that joy does not always look loud. Sometimes it looks like concentration, stillness, pride, or a child who suddenly wants to clap.
  • Follow the children's lead when you can. They are showing you what creates joy for them; you just need to pay attention.

Whether we are guiding a line of excited preschoolers down a long hallway or navigating our own stressful daily routines, joy isn't a distraction from our goals—it is the shared vehicle that helps us reach them, turning everyday resistance into connection.

Source: Literacy@Play; used with permission.

In this series, we’re collaborating with Jenny Millinger, Associate Artistic Director at Childsplay Theatre Company in Tempe, Arizona, and Lauren van Huisstede and Katie Bernstein, researchers from Arizona State University (ASU), to explore the role of the arts and joy in learning and well-being. This intersection of joy, learning, and the arts is at the heart of their work at Literacy@Play, a research-practice partnership between ASU and Childsplay. We explore what science tells us about joy, why the arts are uniquely positioned to spark it, and how intentionally cultivating joyful experiences can transform the way we learn, work, and live.

item.title: Why We're Starting to Take Brain Health More Seriously
item.description:
Diet

Why We're Starting to Take Brain Health More Seriously

The science on brain-health eating isn't new; what's changing is why we care.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Brain health is no longer just about aging; consumers want better focus, memory, and mental clarity today.
  • The Mediterranean, DASH, and MIND diets highlight the connection between heart and brain health.
  • Nutrition, exercise, sleep, and healthy habits all play a role in lifelong cognitive health.

For years, when people discussed brain health, they spoke of aging, of memory loss, of Alzheimer’s disease. Today, the conversation is changing.

Younger generations—in their 30s and 40s, for example—speak of brain fog and mental exhaustion, specifically in terms of lack of concentration and memory. Elderly people also wonder how to maintain their memory so they can remain independent and carry on with their daily lives.

Consumers of all ages are also becoming increasingly aware of the link between their nutrition and their brain health. Yet, while 88 percent of adults over 40 believe that maintaining brain health as we age is important, only 9 percent of us claim to have a lot of knowledge on the subject.

Why Brain Health Matters More Than Ever

I believe several factors have contributed to the rise of interest in brain health.

Many families have personally experienced the serious, often emotionally and financially painful, impacts of someone with Alzheimer’s disease. That disease has become more personal.

Research supports the notion that a host of factors—including nutrition, physical activity, sleep, and cardiovascular health—can affect how our brains function as we age.

Therefore, we've shifted from wanting to maintain memory in old age to wanting to protect cognitive health today.

Three Diets, One Important Message

Dietary approaches that are said to improve brain health are not new.

Mediterranean-style diets have been studied in relation to cardiovascular disease for decades. Traditionally, these types of diets are vegetable- and fruit-dense. They include whole grains, legumes, nuts and seeds, and olive oil, with fish occasionally.

The DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) was developed in the 1990s to help lower blood pressure, largely by decreasing one's daily intake of saturated fat and sodium. The diet consists of a variety of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, and more.

These newer approaches—including the MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay), launched by researchers in 2015 to aid in brain health—concentrate on greens, berries, tree nuts, and olive oil, in addition to other key foods.

Why is this important?

Research has increasingly revealed that heart health equals brain health. How the brain functions depends on healthy blood vessels in order to receive the oxygen and nutrients it requires.

High blood pressure as well as diabetes are known to increase the risk of cognitive decline.

article continues after advertisement

A randomized three-year clinical study published in 2023 did not find significantly greater benefit for cognitive function in subjects following the MIND diet compared with an alternative dietary approach that included calorie restriction, behavioral counseling, and other elements.

More recently, in 2025, the U.S. POINTER trial found that participants who followed a structured program of a MIND-style diet, physical activity, and cognitive and social activities, as well as cardiovascular health monitoring and support, experienced modestly greater gains in some cognitive tests than those who followed a less intense program.

However, it is clear that when looking to support cognitive health, it is best to consider more than just individual nutrients or foods.

Brain Health Is More Than Memory

One of the bigger changes I’m noticing is that, as opposed to asking for ways to improve their memory, consumers are seeking help to enhance their mental clarity; in other words, to improve their focus and energy.

Feeling foggy today does not mean you are developing dementia down the road. This decline in concentration is often associated with poor sleep, excess stress, certain prescription medications, hormonal imbalances, and nutritional deficiencies.

Eating more blueberries or taking a brain health supplement will not solve all of the causes of brain fog.

As a registered dietitian, I am always interested in the reason why someone wants to take a certain supplement. What do they hope that it will do for them? Are they trying to improve their focus for the remainder of the day? Do they have concerns with their memory? Are they looking to support healthy aging?

These are different goals and so require different conversations.

What Can You Do Today?

Supporting brain health doesn't have to be expensive or complicated to implement into your daily life. Here are ways to get started:

  • Incorporate more nutrient-dense foods into your diet. Add a variety of colorful vegetables, different types of berries, beans, whole grains, healthy fats, and a sufficient amount of protein.
  • Get moving regularly. Find activities that strengthen your muscles and help boost cardiovascular fitness.
  • Get enough sleep. This helps ensure optimal learning, memory, and attention.
  • Explore other healthy habits. Maintaining social connections, managing stress, and doing mentally stimulating activities all support the brain, too.
article continues after advertisement

While supplements can help to address specific nutritional requirements, no single ingredient can replace the importance of healthy habits.

The Bigger Picture

For too long, protecting brain health has been viewed as something to worry about only when things start to go wrong.

Simply having a longer life is not the end goal. What matters is maintaining good physical and mental function, so we can enjoy those extra years.

You don’t need to follow a separate set of guidelines for brain health; just an overall set of guidelines that includes your brain.

item.title: Why Some Gay Men Feel They Have to Be the Best
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Why Some Gay Men Feel They Have to Be the Best

How growing up gay can turn achievement into a lifelong search for acceptance.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Some gay men learn to rely on achievement and appearance as protection against rejection.
  • The need to prove our worth can persist long after we've come out and found acceptance.
  • Letting go of needing approval doesn't mean giving up ambition or the satisfaction of doing something well.

I must have been 8 or 9 when I first became obsessed with The Little Mermaid. I had the VHS, the cassette tape, the easy piano sheet music—you name it, I owned it. And one of my favorite pastimes was to take a cushion from the couch, place it on my back with a green macramé shawl holding it in place, and perform "Under the Sea" for my entire family. And yes, you better believe this white Jewish child did the full Jamaican accent. My family adored it. I was asked to do command performances. It was one of the first songs I learned to play on the piano just so I could accompany myself. And while there's nothing wrong with a child soaking up that validation, I think there was something else going on. I didn't want to be Sebastian the crab; I wanted to be Ariel.

I wanted to find a prince washed up on a beach and sing to him until he fell in love with me. I wanted him to see beyond my voice and care for the person underneath. I wanted my family to celebrate our unorthodox marriage with rainbows. I knew that wasn't "normal"—I watched enough Sally Jessy Raphael and Jerry Springer to know that those people were always the butt of the joke. Family vacations to Palm Springs always included snide comments about "the boys" in town.

Looking back, it’s so clear to me what I was learning. I couldn’t control the way my family would react if they found out I was gay. But I could control how well I sang, how hard I worked, how much praise I earned. I had to be the best singer, the most committed performer. If I could get them all to love me enough for my accomplishments, then maybe when they found out I was queer they could somehow overlook that part of me and love me despite it. Ariel was willing to trade her voice for a chance at love, but I was making a different bargain with mine.

The Bargain We Make to Be Loved

It turns out I’m not alone here. In a study inspired by Andrew Tobias’ memoir The Best Little Boy in the World, researchers Pachankis and Hatzenbuehler explored how growing up gay informs how men understand their value. They found that young queer men were more likely than their straight peers to derive their self-worth from their performance and their looks, especially if they had spent a long time closeted or experienced anti-LGBTQ+ stigma growing up. When you can’t control whether or not your friends and family will accept you for who you truly are, you find other things you can control. Your grades. Your looks. Your career. Maybe if you surround yourself with enough markers of external success, they’ll all love you despite your queerness.

But what happens when we don’t need the shield anymore? If you’re like me, you grew up, you came out, and you found that the people who actually mattered loved you for exactly who you are. Maybe you crafted a career, made friends, found a partner, and built a life that seemed unimaginable to your younger self. But the little boy who believed he had to be the best in order to be loved hasn’t gone away. He didn’t get the memo. He’s still pushing you to get to the gym, to find the next accomplishment, to reach the next step in your career. He’s still living by the same rules, just wearing grown-up clothes.

article continues after advertisement

I’m not trying to say that there’s anything wrong with wanting to be good at something. I love to sing, especially with an adoring audience. I feel a sense of pride when a session with a client goes particularly well. But there’s a difference between enjoying the satisfaction of a job well done and needing that rush to know that you’re OK. When our worth is on the line, there will always be something more to do. The praise feels great for a moment, but we spend our lives chasing more applause. Sometimes I feel like I’ve spent much of my adult life collecting evidence that I deserve love but never actually being convinced by any of it.

When Being Good Enough Is Enough

Frankly, I’m exhausted trying to prove this to little me. And so I’ve decided to try something new. Now, it would be so easy to say that the answer is more self-love, but then you’d just go out there and become the best at self-love there ever was. Down, Best Little Boy. Down! Actually, I think the answer is defiance. When I notice that familiar urge to prove my worth, I’m going to see what happens if I just let it be. Don’t get me wrong, I’m not giving up my ambition or pretending that being good at something doesn’t matter to me. But I’m no longer interested in making that a condition for whether or not I deserve to be loved. I’m going to allow myself to let someone down. I’m going to be just so-so at something. I’m going to let people see parts of me that are mediocre, at best. Laying down the shield feels really dangerous, but I’m ready to try.

That little boy with the couch cushion on his back loved performing so much, and I’d never dream of taking that joy away from him. I’d ask him to reconsider the Jamaican accent, but there are some things we just can’t take back. What I want to release him from is the belief that he needed to give his family a reason to love him once they learned the truth. Ariel gave up her voice because she thought that was the cost of loving who she loved. I spent a lifetime pushing myself to make mine stronger for much the same reason.

article continues after advertisement

These days when I sing, I still love the applause. I’m just trying to remember that the people who love me will still be there, whether or not I sing an encore.

item.title: The Gift of a Page
item.description:
Resilience

The Gift of a Page

Personal Perspective: The gift of a lifetime: One journal, 50 years of recovery.

Posted October 24, 2026

Finally getting a chance to say thank-you to the woman who gave me my first journal.
Source: AI generated/Shuttershock

Fifty years ago, when I was 17 and in rehab, my therapist gave me a journal. Her name was Norma. She suggested that I write one page every night. At the time, I barely knew who I was or where my life was headed. I was learning about myself and about recovery. I had no road map and little reason to believe things would work out. I never imagined a journal would become part of my life for the next five decades.

I didn’t write every day. Some nights I wrote for an hour. Other nights the journal just sat there. There were years I barely opened it. But I never stopped writing; I always came back. I couldn’t really tell you why. It just helped.

Today, I have 81 journals. Their pages are filled with pieces of a life of recovery, love, hope, growth, loss, and change. When I look at them, I don’t just see words on pages. I see a woman figuring it out. The journals speak of fear, hope, heartbreak, despair, friendship, grief, anger, joy, and all the feelings that make up a life. Some were written when I was struggling to understand myself, trying to name things I couldn’t quite name yet. Others were written as I became a therapist, a mother, a psychologist, and a partner. Depending on my moods, my handwriting would change. As did my words. As I grew, my understanding of myself deepened, and my life took turns I never could have anticipated. Through it all, I persisted. Page by page, I kept showing up for myself.

For decades, Norma remained part of the beginning of my recovery story. I remembered what she had given me, but I had no idea where she was or whether I would ever see her again. Then, 50 years later, I found her online. I called her. I don’t know exactly what I expected when she answered. I only knew I wanted to tell her how my life had unfolded. That I had stayed clean and sober since rehab. That I had become a therapist. That I had a life beyond my wildest dreams. And that the journal she gave me had multiplied into 81. I wanted her to know that her small suggestion stayed with me. Our conversation was emotional. Norma was surprised I had found her after all those years and even more amazed I had called.

During her career, she counseled many clients without knowing which seeds would take root and which wouldn’t. Most of the time, we never find out. We may remember a client, a session, or a particular moment. But the person sitting across from us may carry something from that encounter long after the session ends, the next year, or the next chapter of their lives.

What feels like a small moment to us might be something a client carries for years. Sometimes it is a word, a new perspective, a question, or a journal that opens a door. We don’t often get to see how deeply we have touched another person. However, if we’re fortunate, a former client calls and lets us know.

Norma gave me a journal. At 17, I didn’t really understand what she was giving me. It took years to figure out what it was. Now I know those pages held things I couldn’t say out loud, the good, the bad, all of it. The journal didn’t judge me. And neither did she.

If I could speak to the person I was back then, I would tell her this: Keep writing. Don’t give up. You have no idea what your life will become.

Norma gave me a journal and suggested that I write one page a night. She couldn’t have known that the gift would fill 81 journals and eventually bring us back together.

Thank you, Norma.

item.title: The Effects of Growing Up in an Emotionally Abusive Family
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

The Effects of Growing Up in an Emotionally Abusive Family

Learning the effects of an EAF can benefit you in multiple ways.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • Learning the effects of being raised in an emotionally abusive family can explain many troubling behaviors.
  • Childhood emotional abuse can impair self-trust, emotional regulation, and adult relationships.
  • The family scapegoat may be the first to recognize abuse and seek help.

Learning the short- and long-term effects of growing up in an emotionally abusive family will help you in several ways. It will help you determine whether you grew up in such an environment; it can explain why you suffer from certain problems and why you've acted in troubling ways; and it can explain why you have felt the way you have—about yourself, your parents, and the rest of your family.

Sources of Emotional Abuse Within a Family

If you were raised in an emotionally abusive family (please refer to my previous post to help determine this), then the damage you experienced may have come from:

  • Witnessing the abuse of one parent toward another
  • Witnessing the abuse of both parents against each other
  • Experiencing emotional abuse first-hand from one or both parents
  • Experiencing a sibling emotionally abusing you
  • Being the target or scapegoat of all family members

In addition, the daily environment of experiencing and/or witnessing emotional abuse has a cumulative effect on your self-esteem, your ability to trust your perceptions, and most importantly, your ability to interact with others in a healthy way.

Short-Term Effects of Childhood Emotional Abuse

Short-term effects of growing up in an emotionally abusive environment include:

  • Nightmares
  • Severe anxiety
  • Depression
  • Anger
  • Irritability
  • A sense of helplessness
  • Behavior problems
  • Clinginess

All these effects continue or worsen the longer children experience emotional abuse, either personally or by witnessing it. There is no such thing as children “getting used to” observing one parent constantly criticize, belittle, accuse, control, make fun of, or blame their partner. In fact, the longer a child witnesses these behaviors, the more they suffer.

This can set the stage for more long-term problems, such as those listed below.

Long-Term Effects of Childhood Emotional Abuse

The following is a list of the damaging long-term effects caused by growing up in an emotionally abusive family. Note which items you relate to.

  1. Attachment issues. This includes difficulties with intimacy, including trusting others; difficulty forming healthy and stable relationships (many survivors continue to be abused or to be abusive in their adult relationships); difficulties with conflict resolution (including a fear of conflict); a fear of abandonment; or extreme clinginess.
  2. Lowered self-esteem and harm to one's sense of self.
  3. Feelings of being unwanted, unloved, worthless, and flawed.
  4. Debilitating shame.
  5. Difficulties regulating emotions.
  6. Mental illness or personality disorders. Those who experienced emotional abuse as a child are more likely to be diagnosed with at least one mental illness, such as severe depression or anxiety, or with a personality disorder such as borderline personality disorder or narcissistic personality disorder.
  7. An increased risk of self-harm, including suicide.
  8. Substance abuse (alcohol, drugs, nicotine) as a way to cope with overwhelming feelings. It has also been shown that there is a connection between experiencing emotional abuse as a child and developing substance abuse disorders.
  9. A tendency to repeat the trauma. People who are abused as children are more likely to abuse their own children than those who did not experience abuse.
  10. Lags in emotional and cognitive development.

It can be overwhelming to read the above lists. But it can also be encouraging. Finally, you have an explanation for some of your most troubling behaviors and feelings.

Family Denial Can Get in the Way of Healing

Unfortunately, you are unlikely to get any help or validation from your family, including from your siblings. Parents tend to be understandably defensive, and even siblings who experienced the same treatment and witnessed the same behavior in your parents can go into denial, insisting that your family was a safe, supportive one, when you know, in fact, that it wasn’t. You can expect your family members to not only be unhelpful but to actively stand together to deny any problems in the family and, in essence, get in the way of healing.

The good news is that, in spite of the denial and lack of validation you receive from your family, there is hope for your healing; the first step being to face the truth about your upbringing and how it affected you.

Most importantly, you need to come to understand that you are not the problem. In fact, it is very possible that you are the healthiest member of the family. There is often one family member in an abusive family who recognizes the problem, and this person is often the family scapegoat—the one everyone in the family blames for all the family problems. This person is often the first one to reach out for help.

Ask for Support That Doesn't Minimize Your Experience

It’s bad enough to have to grow up having an emotionally abusive parent—one who is overly critical, controlling, or neglectful, one who is verbally abusive, smothering, or dismissive—but when you have an emotionally abusive family, it is almost unbearable. There is no one to turn to for help or support.

Don’t make this true for you today. Reach out for help, even if it is just by telling your partner or a close friend. If they try to help by telling you that all families have problems, or to look at how well you turned out, or any other attempt to minimize or ignore the damage you suffered, tell them something like this: “I just need you to listen. You don’t have to try to solve this problem for me. You don’t have to try to take my pain away. Just let me talk, let me tell you how learning about this information and remembering this makes me feel.”

If anyone, including family members, tries to tell you that what you now realize or what you remember is not true, this is not the person to share this information with. Abusive parents often do what is called “gaslighting,” where they lie, deny, or minimize your experience and your feelings. Don’t let anyone in your present life do that to you.

Finally, if you can afford it, seek out a good therapist, one who specializes in trauma if possible. If you can't afford therapy, my new book, Adult Children of Emotionally Abusive Families, will help.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Downside of Casual Dating
item.description:
Relationships

The Downside of Casual Dating

How ambiguous relationships reduce relational quality, and how to improve.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • "Consensual non-monogamy” often involves ambiguity and misunderstanding.
  • Infidelity is difficult to define outside of the boundaries of an exclusive relationship.
  • Relational boundaries are blurred within casual relationships.

Many singles are not in a rush to become couples. That is a positive attitude, because taking it slow produces quality, healthy relationships built on trust, honesty, and compatibility. But building healthy monogamous relationships does not involve dating more than one potential paramour at a time. Open relationships are open to interpretation, which produces problems. Research explains.

Source: aoyon rahman/Pixabay

Boundary Ambiguity

Simone Schneider (2025) explored boundary transgressions within the context of open romantic relationships. She defines open relationships as a type of “consensual non-monogamy” form of intimacy, and acknowledges they often involve ambiguity or disagreements over boundaries, and boundary violations. This is particularly true among young adults. Studying a population from England of 19 participants with an average age of 25 years, all of whom had completed or pursued university education, she argues that infidelity serves as a cultural range of behavior that young adults use to navigate the ambiguity of open relationships and set moral and symbolic boundaries.

The value of exploring relational boundaries does not end with youth. Casual dating often implies non-serious relationships, which many people interpret to involve multiple dating partners. Schneider’s research included an examination of this issue, studying one of the most prevalent sources of misunderstanding among any adult relationships—the ambiguity of unsolidified boundaries. Practical examples might include a dating partner freely discussing other romantic relationships or being seen in public with different partners, making no effort to hide any of the relationships. Many daters would not accept this behavior, even when they initially “agreed” to be non-exclusive. Emotional responses within open relationships involve another point Schneider makes, which is that perceived boundary violations reflect uneven desires for monogamy.

Defining Terms of Endearment

Ideally, dating partners are on the same page regarding romantic intentions, values, and ideas about exploring romantic alternatives. This conversation should come up sooner rather than later within developing relationships, where potential paramours are navigating the anticipatory stage of romance. Boundaries are also formed implicitly, as both parties express their intentions regarding exclusivity with each other, and through public displays of affection and terminology—such as introducing each other as a “boyfriend,” “girlfriend,” or “better half.” Problems arise when symbols of growing intimacy are absent or only occur in private.

Defining terms also prevents misunderstanding. Schneider notes that within consensual non-monogamous relationships, couples defined infidelity as behavior that violates previously agreed-upon relational arrangements. She also found that within open relationships, infidelity was viewed as involving dishonesty, secrecy, and violations of trust. Yet labels matter too. Schneider’s study participants often referred to their partners as their “boyfriend” or “girlfriend,” although they had permission to date others. As a practical matter, we can anticipate this creates unrealistic role expectations because terms of exclusivity are usually reserved for exclusive relationships.

Meeting of the Hearts and Minds

The best relationships start slow but proceed along a steady path of mutual understanding. Among partners who agree they are permitted to date multiple people, imbalanced emotional investment results in an uneven playing field. This produces disappointment, disenchantment, and heartache—all of which reduce relational quality. The best pairings involve openness, chemistry, and good communication. A friends-first approach permits couples to get to know each other without the pressure of labeling their relationship, moving forward with a healthy bond, ready to blossom when the time is right.

item.title: It's Good to Be Bored Sometimes
item.description:
Boredom

It's Good to Be Bored Sometimes

Personality science partly explains our constant search for stimulation.

Posted October 24, 2026

Key points
  • People higher in extraversion tend to seek out more excitement and stimulation.
  • Constantly escaping boredom can make it harder to tolerate periods of low stimulation.
  • Practicing boredom can help people become more flexible in how they respond to it.

Think about the last time you had some downtime. Maybe you were standing in line at the grocery store, sitting in a doctor's waiting room, or waiting for a friend to arrive at a restaurant. What did you do?

If you're like most people, you probably reached for your phone. Within seconds, you were able to check your email, scroll through social media, or catch up on the news. What might once have been a few minutes of quiet downtime is now an opportunity to entertain yourself.

We’ve gotten really good at eliminating boredom from our lives. But what are the costs of constantly seeking out something to occupy our attention?

The Personality Behind Stimulation-Seeking

Some people have a greater appetite for stimulation than others. Although we often associate extraversion with sociability, this trait is actually broader than that. Indeed, those who are higher in extraversion are more inclined to seek out activity and entertainment.

Like all personality traits, extraversion exists on a continuum. Being fairly extraverted is generally seen as a good thing, but at the extremely high end, there can be some consequences. When the drive for stimulation is particularly strong, it can feel nearly impossible to tolerate situations that aren't especially exciting or engaging. For example, someone might struggle to enjoy a relaxing weekend at home, feel restless when they have nothing planned, or have difficulty sticking with tasks that are important but not particularly interesting.

When Boredom Becomes Something to Escape

Boredom can be uncomfortable. And for someone with a strong appetite for stimulation, a quiet evening in or a tedious work task can feel especially unpleasant. The natural response is to find something to fill that time. The more uncomfortable boredom feels, the more motivated we become to escape it.

Each time we seek out stimulation, whether that’s from scrolling through TikTok or hanging out with a friend, we get immediate relief from boredom. This relief is reinforcing, making us more likely to seek out a distraction the next time boredom strikes. Over time, we can become so accustomed to filling every available moment that even brief periods without something to do start to feel increasingly uncomfortable.

But when we fill every available moment with activity or entertainment, we lose opportunities to reflect on our experiences, process what's happened during the day, or let our minds wander. Sometimes our best ideas come when we're not actively trying to accomplish anything. Constantly seeking stimulation can stifle creativity and prevent our ability to learn from past setbacks.

Our discomfort with boredom can also lead us to make choices that aren't particularly good for us. Maybe you agree to go out with friends even though you're exhausted and have an early morning because the thought of everyone having fun without you feels unbearable. Or you fill your weekend with activities even though what you really need is a chance to rest.

In these situations, the problem isn't enjoying excitement or being social. It's that simply avoiding boredom has started to influence your decisions, sometimes at the expense of things you value more.

Practice Being Bored

If you've gotten used to filling every spare moment with something entertaining, the idea of intentionally doing nothing might sound pretty unappealing. At the same time, learning to be more comfortable with periods of low stimulation will allow you to be intentional about how you spend your time—rather than keeping busy just to escape discomfort.

Start by looking for small opportunities to leave time unfilled. Maybe you take a walk without listening to a podcast, resist the urge to check your phone while waiting in line, or spend a few minutes sitting outside without doing anything in particular. Notice what happens when you don't immediately respond to the urge to entertain yourself.

You might feel restless, impatient, or tempted to find something more interesting to do. That's okay. Rather than immediately acting on those feelings, see what happens if you give yourself a few minutes to let them ride. You may discover that the discomfort is manageable and that you don't actually need to do anything to make it go away.

You can also practice this when making decisions about how to spend your time. The next time you're tempted to make plans simply because you don't want to miss out, ask yourself whether the activity is something you genuinely want to do or whether you're trying to avoid an evening without much excitement. Sometimes going out will be values-aligned. Other times, staying home might be the better choice.

Make Room for Less Stimulation

There's nothing wrong with enjoying a busy schedule, exciting experiences, or frequent opportunities to connect with others. For people who are naturally high in extraversion, these activities can be an important source of enjoyment and fulfillment.

But even the personality traits that generally serve us well can create problems when they become too extreme. If your need for stimulation makes it difficult to rest, reflect, or spend time alone, it may be worth experimenting with turning that particular aspect of your personality down a notch.
